title: Why Chicken Bones Turn Pink (It's Not What You Think)
description: Pink bones don't mean your chicken is undercooked -- here's the real food science behind it. AI-narrated commentary breaking down a common kitchen myth in under a minute. #shorts #foodscience #lifehacks

hook_candidates.text: Why do chicken bones still look pink even after the meat's fully cooked?
That pink tint by the bone isn't blood, and it's not proof your chicken is raw.
Pink near the bone does NOT mean your chicken is undercooked, despite what everyone assumes.

beats.text: Why do chicken bones still look pink even after the meat's fully cooked?
beats.broll_query: cooked chicken drumstick pink bone close up

beats.text: In young broiler chickens, the bones are still porous, so pigment from the marrow seeps out into the bone during cooking.
beats.broll_query: raw chicken bone marrow close up

beats.text: That pigment can tint the bone and nearby meat pink or reddish, but it has nothing to do with how well the meat is cooked.
beats.broll_query: chicken meat near bone reddish tint

beats.text: The only real test is a meat thermometer hitting one-sixty-five degrees at the thickest part, not the color of the bone.
So next time you spot a pink bone, that's just biology, not a mistake -- comment if you've ever tossed good chicken because of this.
